item.title: 'Power of disorder' tames CF₄, a semiconductor greenhouse gas that can persist for 50,000 years
item.description: Problem: CF4, used in chip fabrication, is over 6,000x more potent than CO2 and persists ~50,000 years. Catalysts meant to break it down corrode and clump under the heat, moisture, and fluorine involved, losing effectiveness fast. Approach: KAIST researchers mixed five metals (Al, Zn, Ga, Ni, Co) evenly into one aluminate crystal structure, using 'entropy stabilization' -- structural disorder that resists clumping -- to keep the catalyst intact under harsh conditions. Result: In an 800C, 150-hour accelerated test, conventional catalyst conversion fell from 93% to 48%; the new catalyst held at 98% to 92%, roughly 2.3x higher intrinsic activity overall. Why it matters: A catalyst that keeps working under real fab conditions turns a lab result into something semiconductor plants could actually deploy to cut a very potent, very persistent greenhouse gas. Jargon: Entropy stabilization -- using atomic disorder to keep a mixed-metal structure from separating into simpler phases. Aluminate -- a compound where metals bond around an aluminum-oxygen framework. Dry etching -- using reactive gas (not liquid) to carve circuit patterns into a wafer. Oxygen isotope tracing -- tagging oxygen atoms to track their path through a chemical reaction.

item.title: A Split Keyboard Designed for Human Hands
item.description: Problem: Standard keyboards still copy the 19th-century typewriter layout -- flat rows, a shared spacebar hogging both thumbs -- which doesn't match how hands and fingers actually move. Approach: Paul iterated roughly 50 times on a split, columnar keyboard where each finger's column is angled and spaced for that finger specifically (ring finger keys raised, index columns angled inward), using low-profile switches to keep it compact and portable. Result: A 36-key layout where each thumb covers three keys -- space plus two 'layer' keys -- replacing dozens of rarely-reachable keys with layered combinations. Why it matters: It's a concrete example of ergonomics-first hardware design overturning a century-old default that most people never question. Jargon: Columnar layout -- keys stacked in straight columns instead of offset rows. Layer key -- a modifier that remaps other keys to a second function, like a hardware Shift. Low-profile switch -- a shorter mechanical key switch for slimmer builds.
